paragraphs: Rating teams requires a model that can interpret competition outcomes when the participating groups have different sizes or several teams finish tied. This paper introduces a probabilistic rating system built on TrueSkill, targeting these situations as problems that the existing system needs to handle more effectively.

The central change is to the factor graph structure. A factor graph expresses how the quantities in a probabilistic model relate to one another, so changing its structure changes how competition results inform ratings. The authors also provide detailed inference algorithms for the revised structure, explaining how to carry out the calculations required by the new system.

The reported experiments show a significant improvement over TrueSkill. This supports the proposed combination of a revised model structure and corresponding inference procedures for team competitions. The contribution is therefore both a new way to organize the rating problem and algorithms for using that organization, with multiway ties and variable team sizes motivating the redesign.
icml-2011-a-new-bayesian-rating-system-f.tldr: A revised TrueSkill-based probabilistic model improves team ratings while addressing multiway ties and variable team sizes.

paragraphs: Latent variable models explain observed data through variables that are not directly measured. Learning their parameters often relies on methods such as expectation maximization, which search locally and can settle at local optima. This paper proposes a fast spectral learning algorithm for latent variable models arranged in arbitrary tree structures.

A central result concerns how much observed information is needed to reconstruct the model's observable behavior. The authors show that the joint distribution of observed variables can be recovered from marginal distributions involving triples of observed variables, regardless of the tree's maximum degree. In other words, the reconstruction does not require larger observed groups simply because some tree nodes have many connections.

The algorithm avoids local minima and is evaluated on synthetic and real data. With large training sets, its performance is comparable to or better than expectation maximization while running orders of magnitude faster. The training-size qualification matters: the reported comparison specifically supports the method's combination of speed and performance in that setting.
icml-2011-a-spectral-algorithm-for-laten.tldr: A spectral algorithm learns latent tree models without local minima, reconstructing observed distributions from triples of variables.

paragraphs: Relational learning concerns data described through connections, potentially involving several kinds of relationships. This paper proposes representing such data with a three-way tensor and learning a factorization of that tensor. The factorization provides latent components through which the model can organize the information contained in the different relationships.

The key contribution is collective learning through those latent components. Rather than treating every relationship as an isolated learning problem, the model can use its shared internal representation to connect their learning. The authors explain this capability theoretically and supply an efficient algorithm for computing the factorization, linking the modeling idea to a practical procedure.

Experiments on a new dataset and an established entity-resolution dataset support the discussion of collective learning. On common benchmarks, the method also obtains results that match or improve on the compared state-of-the-art relational learning approaches while requiring significantly less computation. These findings support both the usefulness of the latent sharing and the computational efficiency of the proposed factorization.
icml-2011-a-three-way-model-for-collecti.tldr: A three-way tensor factorization shares latent components across relationships, achieving competitive relational learning results with faster computation.

paragraphs: Indian Buffet Process models can discover underlying features without requiring their number to be specified in advance. The difficulty is inference: sampling can be expensive and slow to converge, while variational methods can be difficult to design and remain costly on large datasets. The paper targets applications that only need a high-probability feature assignment.

For these applications, the authors use beam search to obtain fast, approximate maximum a posteriori estimates of the latent feature assignment matrix. The goal is a likely configuration under the posterior, rather than a collection of posterior samples. When samples are needed, the resulting estimates can instead provide sensible starting points for Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithms.

Experiments across several datasets suggest that these search procedures offer a computationally viable alternative to Gibbs sampling, particle filtering, and variational inference for IBP models. They also perform better than heuristics such as greedy search. The findings support approximate MAP search as a useful option when that form of inference matches the application's needs.
icml-2011-beam-search-based-map-estimate.tldr: Beam search provides fast approximate MAP feature assignments for Indian Buffet Process models and useful starting points for posterior sampling.

paragraphs: Selective sampling addresses an online learning problem in which the learner chooses when to request a label. Its performance therefore has two related dimensions: how often its predictions are wrong and how often it asks for supervision. This paper studies algorithms that use regularized least squares as their underlying classifier.

Existing algorithms of this kind can work well empirically, and some already have guarantees on mistakes and label requests. The authors refine and broaden those guarantees, then propose variants with better observed behavior. Their guarantees apply under substantially more general conditions, extending the circumstances in which the algorithms have formal support.

The paper also shows how to combine a particular least-squares-based selective sampler with a generic gradient-based classifier. This separates the choice of which labels to request from the classifier used to learn predictions. The resulting hybrid algorithms retain combined performance guarantees, making the contribution relevant both to improved least-squares methods and to selective sampling systems that use other gradient-based prediction rules.
icml-2011-better-algorithms-for-selectiv.tldr: Improved selective sampling algorithms broaden mistake and query guarantees and support hybrids with gradient-based classifiers.

paragraphs: A classifier may have access to many features but only be allowed to inspect a limited number for each new example. This paper studies that prediction-time constraint. Its focus is feature-efficient classification: making a decision while controlling the amount of feature information examined for an individual test case.

The proposed approach modifies a weighted ensemble such as AdaBoost by sampling hypotheses from its final predictor. This uses the ensemble's learned weighting to guide a smaller prediction computation. The authors also extend the approach to situations where features have different inspection costs, so the problem involves more than simply counting how many features are used.

The paper proves correctness of the algorithms and bounds the number of samples required for specified error rates. Those bounds connect the amount of sampled prediction work to the desired accuracy. Experiments further support the methods' effectiveness. Together, the contributions show how an ensemble can be adapted to feature budgets, including budgets where individual observations have unequal costs.
icml-2011-boosting-on-a-budget-sampling-.tldr: Sampling hypotheses from weighted ensembles enables prediction under feature budgets, with error-related sample bounds and support for unequal feature costs.

paragraphs: An auto-encoder learns features while trying to reconstruct its input. This paper adds a penalty that directly discourages the encoder's activations from changing too strongly when the input changes locally. The penalty uses the Frobenius norm of the encoder's Jacobian, a matrix describing the sensitivity of its activations to input changes.

The authors show that this penalty contracts the local representation space and produces robust features. Empirically, the representation better captures directions of variation associated with the data's lower-dimensional nonlinear manifold, while becoming more invariant to most directions orthogonal to it. This distinguishes preserving meaningful local variation from simply suppressing every possible change.

Across a range of datasets, the method matches or exceeds other regularized and denoising auto-encoders. The paper also explains connections between these approaches, positioning the penalty as a link between deterministic and nondeterministic auto-encoders. Using the learned features to initialize a multilayer perceptron yields state-of-the-art classification errors on the evaluated datasets and surpasses other pretraining methods.
icml-2011-contractive-auto-encoders-expl.tldr: A sensitivity penalty helps auto-encoders learn locally robust features that improve classification when used for pretraining.

paragraphs: Graphical models can contain both discrete choices and continuous quantities restricted to bounded ranges. This paper extends convex max-product inference to such hybrid models. The target is the maximum a posteriori assignment: the combination of variable values with the greatest posterior probability. The authors derive conditions under which their approach is guaranteed to find it.

Continuous variables create a representation problem because the messages passed during inference are functions. The paper investigates a multigrid method that represents these functions through piecewise constant values. This approach provides the theoretical guarantees, but the authors describe it as impractical, motivating a more usable algorithm inspired by the same development.

That practical proposal is a particle convex max-product method. On protein folding, it significantly outperforms existing particle methods and achieves performance comparable to the state of the art while using less prior knowledge. The guarantee-bearing multigrid construction and the empirically evaluated particle algorithm play distinct roles: one establishes the theoretical approach, while the other demonstrates its practical promise.
icml-2011-convex-max-product-over-compac.tldr: Hybrid convex max-product inference leads to conditional MAP guarantees and a practical particle algorithm with strong protein-folding results.

paragraphs: A Bayes Point machine performs binary classification by estimating the posterior mean of classifier parameters as an approximation to the Bayes-optimal classifier. Computing that mean is intractable in the setting considered. Earlier methods address the difficulty through message passing that approximates the parameter posterior with a Gaussian distribution.

This paper investigates message-passing alternatives that avoid that Gaussian approximation. Its enabling contribution is a computational shortcut based on linear multiple-choice knapsack problems. The shortcut reduces the cost of computing Bayes Point belief-propagation messages from exponential to linear in the number of data features, making the alternative inference approach substantially more manageable.

Experiments on several real-world UCI datasets show significant improvements in linear classification over both soft-margin support vector machines and Expectation Propagation Bayes Point machines. These results provide empirical support for the alternative message calculations. The contribution combines a different treatment of the posterior with a specific complexity reduction, rather than relying on the Gaussian approximation used by previous Bayes Point approaches.
icml-2011-estimating-the-bayes-point-usi.tldr: A knapsack-based shortcut makes non-Gaussian Bayes Point message passing efficient and improves linear classification on several UCI datasets.

paragraphs: A weighted majority vote combines basis functions into a single prediction rule. This paper chooses their weights by minimizing a risk bound called the C-bound. The bound depends on the first two moments of the combined predictor's margin on training data, bringing both its average margin and its second-moment behavior into the objective.

The resulting optimization is a quadratic program that can be solved efficiently. The authors develop one version for supervised inductive learning and another for transductive learning. The supervised version is competitive with AdaBoost, MDBoost, and support vector machines, while the transductive version compares well with transductive support vector machines.

The paper also introduces a PAC-Bayes theorem controlling the difference between the true C-bound and its empirical estimate. Unusually, this theorem contains no Kullback-Leibler divergence. Together, the algorithm and theorem connect a bound on majority-vote risk to a tractable weight-selection procedure, with experiments supporting competitiveness in both of the learning settings studied.
icml-2011-from-pac-bayes-bounds-to-quadr.tldr: Minimizing a margin-based risk bound yields efficient quadratic programs for weighted majority votes and a PAC-Bayes theorem without KL divergence.

paragraphs: Value-based reinforcement learning must both estimate how promising situations or actions are and select an action to take. With large action sets, evaluating every candidate can become impractical. This paper argues that efficient action selection needs to shape the value representation itself, rather than being considered only after that representation is chosen.

The authors develop a unified view of state-value and state-action-value functions, leading to a new space-efficient representation. In this representation, action selection can be exponentially faster without using a model. The contribution therefore addresses the cost of making a decision as well as the space required to represent the values supporting it.

The paper also describes how to compute the new value function efficiently using approximate linear programming. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the approach. The stated speed advantage concerns action selection, linking the representation directly to the large-action-set problem; the additional computation method provides a way to learn the quantities needed to use that representation.
icml-2011-generalized-value-functions-fo.tldr: A unified value-function representation supports space-efficient storage and exponentially faster action selection without a model.

paragraphs: This paper studies minimizing a convex objective over large matrices while requiring the solution to have low rank. Low rank restricts the complexity of the matrix representation, but it also makes the optimization problem difficult in general. A convex objective alone does not remove the difficulty introduced by that constraint.

The authors propose an efficient greedy algorithm and establish formal approximation guarantees. Each iteration approximately finds the left and right singular vectors associated with the largest singular value of a particular matrix. The abstract states that this calculation can be performed in linear time, providing the computational basis for handling large matrices.

The approach is relevant to applications including matrix completion for collaborative filtering and robust low-rank matrix approximation. Its significance lies in pairing a scalable iterative calculation with guarantees on approximation quality. The result offers a principled way to work with large low-rank matrix problems while retaining the paper's distinction between efficient approximation and the general difficulty of the constrained optimization task.
icml-2011-large-scale-convex-minimizatio.tldr: A greedy algorithm uses approximate leading singular vectors to scale low-rank matrix optimization while providing approximation guarantees.

paragraphs: This paper introduces deep energy models, which use a deep feedforward neural network to define the energy landscape of a probabilistic model. The network therefore helps determine how the model represents the distribution of data. The work builds on the ability of deep generative models to learn compact and meaningful representations.

A central feature is efficient joint training of all layers. This allows lower layers to adapt as higher layers learn, instead of fixing their behavior through greedy layer-by-layer training. On natural images, the authors report both qualitative and quantitative improvements in generative performance from training multiple layers together.

The paper also extends the model family beyond sigmoidal neural networks. A deep version of a product of Student-t distributions achieves good generative performance, showing that the approach accommodates another modeling form. Finally, a discriminative extension outperforms other fully connected models on NORB object recognition. These results support the approach for both modeling data distributions and learning predictors in the evaluated settings.
icml-2011-learning-deep-energy-models-bb.tldr: Deep energy models enable joint training across layers, improving natural-image generation and supporting a strong object-recognition extension.

paragraphs: Data can have several representations, or views, whose original distances are not directly comparable. This paper learns projections into a shared feature space where Euclidean distance expresses similarity both within a view and across different views. The motivation is cross-media retrieval, where a common distance enables fast nearest-neighbor queries, including hashing-based approaches.

The learning objective brings matching samples close together and pushes nonmatching samples apart, regardless of which views contain them. This makes the desired cross-view relationships part of the geometry being learned. The optimization problem is nonconvex, but the authors explicitly split it into convex and concave parts so that the convex-concave procedure can optimize it efficiently.

Experiments on image retrieval demonstrate that nearest-neighbor retrieval across views is possible with the learned space. The proposed method also improves retrieval accuracy over the evaluated baselines. These results support learning a shared distance as a practical connection between different representations and efficient similarity-based retrieval.
icml-2011-learning-multi-view-neighborho.tldr: Learned projections place different data views in a shared distance space that improves cross-view nearest-neighbor retrieval.

paragraphs: Tree kernels provide ways to compare data organized as trees. This paper surveys them through the mapping-kernels framework, giving a common perspective on methods that can otherwise appear computationally intricate. The authors argue that most existing tree kernels, together with many introduced in the paper, fit into a shared typology.

Within that typology, the computations can be factorized to obtain polynomial-time algorithms. However, the authors emphasize that this computational classification does not by itself make a straightforward implementation practical. Even a polynomial-time method can require prohibitive computation, so the paper addresses implementation efficiency alongside the unifying mathematical framework.

The proposed improvement caches some computations for smaller trees so that they can be reused. Experiments show substantial speedups across the tree kernels considered, and the paper also reports preliminary results on their performance. Its contribution combines organization of the kernel family, efficient factorization, and a reuse strategy that makes those computations more practical.
icml-2011-mapping-kernels-for-trees-65e1.tldr: A mapping-kernel framework unifies tree kernels, while caching smaller-tree computations substantially speeds their evaluation.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to turn high-dimensional data into compact binary codes while preserving similarity. Each learned hash function contributes to a representation made of binary values. The aim is for this compact representation to retain useful information about which original data items resemble one another.

The authors formulate the learning problem as structured prediction with latent variables and a hinge-like loss. This treats code learning as a prediction problem with an explicit loss criterion. The latent variables are part of the formulation, allowing the learning procedure to work with quantities that are not simply supplied as observed target values.

The method is reported to train efficiently on large datasets and to scale well as code lengths increase. It also outperforms the state-of-the-art methods used for comparison. These findings connect the similarity-preservation objective to two practical demands: learning from substantial amounts of data and supporting larger binary representations. The contribution is a learned hashing method that addresses those computational demands alongside predictive quality.
icml-2011-minimal-loss-hashing-for-compa.tldr: A latent structured-prediction formulation learns similarity-preserving binary hashes efficiently for large datasets and longer codes.

paragraphs: Bipartite ranking concerns ordering examples associated with two classes. This paper asks how quickly the excess ranking risk can decrease as training data increases. It focuses on plug-in ranking rules, following results showing that plug-in classifiers can achieve fast, and sometimes super-fast, rates under suitable assumptions.

The authors analyze ranking as a nested continuous family of cost-sensitive classification problems. This viewpoint connects the ranking task to classification problems with varying costs. They identify a global low-noise condition under which certain plug-in ranking rules achieve fast convergence rates, establishing minimax upper bounds on excess ranking risk.

The qualification on the rates is central: the paper establishes fast rates, but not super-fast ones. In the terminology used in the abstract, fast means faster than the inverse square root of sample size, while super-fast means faster than its inverse. The result therefore extends part of the classification picture to ranking under a stated low-noise condition without transferring the strongest classification rate claim.
icml-2011-minimax-learning-rates-for-bip.tldr: Under a global low-noise condition, certain plug-in ranking rules achieve fast, but not super-fast, excess-risk rates.

paragraphs: This paper extends deep unsupervised feature learning from individual data types to multiple modalities, particularly audio and video. It develops training approaches for several multimodal tasks. A key question is whether information from one modality can improve the features learned for another, even when the eventual representation is used for just one.

The authors demonstrate this kind of cross-modality feature learning: having audio and video available during feature learning can produce better video features. They also learn a shared representation connecting the modalities. To test that connection, they train a classifier on audio-only data and evaluate it on video-only data, and perform the reverse transfer as well.

Evaluation uses audio-visual speech classification on CUAVE and AVLetters. The paper reports the best published visual speech classification result on AVLetters and effective shared representation learning. These findings support two related benefits of multimodal training: improving features for an individual modality and learning a representation that supports classification transfer between different input modalities.
icml-2011-multimodal-deep-learning-d0b08.tldr: Joint audio-video learning improves single-modality features and enables classifiers to transfer between audio-only and video-only data.

paragraphs: Some feature-learning architectures produce useful object-recognition features even when their weights remain random and untrained. This paper investigates why that can happen. It separates the contribution of the architecture from the contribution of learned weights, asking how much useful behavior is already present in the arrangement of computations.

The proposed explanation is that certain convolutional pooling architectures can be frequency selective and translation invariant even with random weights. Such properties can therefore arise from the architecture itself. The claim is specific to certain architectures, rather than suggesting that arbitrary networks with random weights will provide useful recognition features.

The authors use this observation to demonstrate extremely fast architecture search: candidate architectures are evaluated with random weights, avoiding the learning process during evaluation. They also show that a substantial fraction of the performance of certain state-of-the-art methods comes from architecture alone. The findings make architecture an explanatory factor in recognition performance and a practical target for faster search.
icml-2011-on-random-weights-and-unsuperv.tldr: Certain convolutional pooling architectures produce useful features with random weights, enabling fast architecture search without training each candidate.

paragraphs: The paper revisits portfolio allocation through the mean-variance framework associated with Markowitz. It identifies a restriction: the approach is approximation-free only for Gaussian stock returns, an assumption the abstract says does not hold in real data. The authors seek a broader mathematical setting that also supports online portfolio learning.

They generalize mean-variance allocation to a mean-divergence model, allowing returns from any exponential family of distributions. This relaxes the Gaussian restriction within a specified family of models. They then develop a general online learning algorithm and prove lower bounds on certainty equivalents, the optimization quantity emphasized in their treatment of the Markowitz framework.

Experiments on four real-world stock markets show the algorithm's ability to track portfolios whose cumulative returns exceed those of the best individual stock by orders of magnitude. This is an empirical tracking result, alongside theoretical bounds on a different stated quantity. The contribution combines a broader return-distribution model, an online algorithm, and analysis aligned with the framework's certainty-equivalent objective.
icml-2011-on-tracking-portfolios-with-ce.tldr: A mean-divergence generalization of Markowitz allocation supports exponential-family returns and online portfolio learning with certainty-equivalent bounds.

paragraphs: In cost-sensitive classification, errors can carry different costs, and here those costs may also depend on the individual example. The paper studies surrogate losses used to learn classifiers for this setting, also described as regression level-set estimation. The central question is whether optimizing the surrogate reliably advances the actual cost-sensitive objective.

The authors give sufficient conditions for a surrogate regret bound to exist. Such a bound connects the gap from optimal surrogate risk to the gap from optimal expected misclassification cost. Consequently, as the surrogate risk approaches its optimum, the expected classification cost also approaches its optimum under the stated conditions.

The sufficient conditions cover example-dependent versions of familiar losses, including hinge and exponential losses. This provides theoretical justification for some algorithms that had already been proposed and points toward other possible algorithms. The result is a guarantee connecting two optimization objectives; its sufficient conditions establish when that connection holds without claiming they are the only conditions under which it could hold.
icml-2011-surrogate-losses-and-regret-bo.tldr: Sufficient conditions connect surrogate optimization to optimal classification cost when error costs depend on individual examples.

paragraphs: Visualizing high-dimensional data requires compressing it into a low-dimensional space while retaining structure useful for exploration. Clusters are one such structure. The paper identifies two problems with existing approaches: crowding can prevent clusters from being preserved, and some methods preserve them only at a single resolution.

Tree preserving embedding uses the topological concept of connectedness to address cluster preservation across resolutions. The idea is to make the grouping structure central to the embedding's objective. The authors prove that their approach preserves clusters at all resolutions, supporting exploration of both broader groupings and finer distinctions within the data.

The performance guarantee applies to finite samples, connecting the theoretical result to the finite datasets encountered in applications. The contribution is therefore a visualization approach with a specific structural guarantee, rather than only a visual assessment of whether a projection looks informative. The paper presents this result as a foundation for more robust practical visualization strategies.
icml-2011-tree-preserving-embedding-748a.tldr: Tree preserving embedding uses connectedness to provably preserve clusters across all resolutions, with guarantees for finite samples.

paragraphs: Multiple kernel learning must balance predictive quality, a sparse solution, and the time needed for optimization. This paper approaches those goals together by designing the regularizer with its optimization algorithm in mind. The resulting formulation combines elements of p-norm and elastic-net regularization, accompanied by a fast stochastic gradient descent method.

The method produces exactly sparse solutions with an adjustable degree of sparsity. Its convergence-rate bound depends only logarithmically on the number of kernels and is independent of the requested sparsity level. These properties connect the choice of a compact solution to an optimization analysis that does not worsen with that sparsity requirement.

The authors also report that the approach is independent of the particular convex loss used and achieves state-of-the-art performance on many classification tasks. The theoretical and empirical results support the joint design strategy: the learning formulation accommodates sparsity and predictive performance while the associated algorithm addresses computational cost. The performance claim remains tied to the classification tasks evaluated.
icml-2011-ultra-fast-optimization-algori.tldr: Jointly designing regularization and optimization yields fast multiple kernel learning with tunable exact sparsity and a logarithmic kernel-count convergence dependence.

paragraphs: Many policy-search algorithms fit a policy by minimizing Kullback-Leibler divergence to a target distribution. This paper emphasizes that the divergence is asymmetric: reversing its direction changes the behavior encouraged by learning. The usual direction attracts the policy toward positively rewarded experiences while neglecting negative experiences, whereas the reversed direction encourages avoidance of negatively rewarded behavior.

The proposed method, Variational Inference for Policy Search, uses this reversed divergence. Its cost-averse policy seeks to avoid reproducing negative experiences while maximizing exploration. The inference also determines settings that would otherwise require an exploration rate or kernel bandwidth, removing the need to specify those quantities separately.

The authors report performance matching state-of-the-art methods and the ability to learn in multiple situations simultaneously. Their robotics application trains a human-like four-link robot to dynamically counterbalance different kinds of pushes. This illustrates the paper's central motivation: changing the distribution-fitting objective can support policy learning across varying situations while automatically determining aspects of exploration.
icml-2011-variational-inference-for-poli.tldr: Reversing KL divergence produces a cost-averse policy-search method that determines exploration settings automatically and learns across multiple situations.

paragraphs: This paper develops variational Bayesian inference for the stick-breaking construction of the beta process. The computational challenge is to work with a prior whose full construction is infinite. The authors derive an alternative representation of the process that is suitable for variational inference, making that representation the foundation of their algorithm.

A second contribution concerns truncation: replacing the infinite construction with a finite one that can be used in computation. The paper provides a bound relating the truncated beta process to its infinite counterpart. This gives a mathematical connection between the finite approximation used in practice and the original probabilistic object, rather than leaving their relationship uncharacterized.

The authors assess the method on two matrix-factorization problems, one using a nonnegative factorization model and the other a linear-Gaussian model. These applications exercise the inference procedure in different modeling settings. Together, the alternative representation, truncation bound, and evaluations establish a route for applying variational inference to this beta-process construction.
icml-2011-variational-inference-for-stic.tldr: An alternative beta-process representation enables variational inference, supported by a truncation bound and two matrix-factorization evaluations.
